title: The Daily Driver - Detailed Japanese Bus Simulation
author: No_Entrepreneur6548
selftext:
The Daily Driver is a detailed bus driving simulator set in Ise and Wakayama Japan. I was inspired to make this tech demo after visiting the region last year. Opus 5.5 has gone a long way in being able to build out highly detailed models and spaces. Here is some helpful tips for people who are looking to start pushing the envelope on this.

1) This game is built on top of Godot. All assets are rendered in Blender. Textures are open source items, and sometimes generated by AI. Voices and station call outs are pipelined through old fashioned windows sound generation.

2) I pushed Opus to find reference shots of the buses in the region, and to push harder over and over on making sure that it was realistic, and that the console worked properly. There are currently 2 buses in the game, with most of their systems working.

3) You can leverage open street maps data, along with google street view to populate large game worlds. The Hongu map is over 36km of terrain along a massive valley in Japan. It includes dozens of stops.

4) Blenders open source people plugin was used to animate the people. Sometimes to hilarious effect, as people do move and fall, when the bus is moving too fast. This lead to AI strapping someone in a wheel chair to the bus and smashing it into traffic to 'make sure' the animation was correct.

5) Create detailed requirements in simulations about the rules for rendering and placing items in your game. This game has some famous landmarks, but for the most part open street map provides the 'location' of buildings and then the game fills in those locations with a best guess.

6) Start your game basic and build up in layers. Towards the end of this you can see the engine simulations. There are additional simulations for tires and cabin temperature. I would not of ever started with that, but its the kind of layering that turns the game from 'drive a bus' to 'carefully manage the customer experience'.

A philosophical point for anyone reading this far. Right now the highest fidelity bus simulator 'barely runs' on most computers. I went down this path for the last few days seeing how far we can go to start saying, 'do we have to accept this?' And the answer is in my view, not for much longer. I am hoping that as we get deeper into these tools that we will find the ability for the open source community to start producing amazing content that is not tied into commercial game engines (DCS/OSMI/Train Sim), and i'm super excited to see what people end up with.

If you have any interest in trying this out I may release it at some point or let others give it a shot.
